prompt: Explain the Electoral College using only NASCAR metaphors. Keep going long after the metaphor stops making sense.
response:
Winning the championship (the Presidency) isn’t just about having the most fans sitting in the grandstands wearing your merchandise across the entire country. That’s the Popular Fan Count, and while it's nice for selling t-shirts, it doesn’t win you the Cup. 

Instead, the championship is decided by a point system scattered across 51 different speedways (the 50 states plus the District of Columbia track). Each speedway is worth a specific number of Championship Laps (Electoral Votes). The number of laps a track is worth depends on how many grandstand seats it has. The massive California Super Speedway is worth 54 laps, while the tiny Wyoming Dirt Track is only worth 3. 

Here’s the catch: almost every single track uses a "winner-take-all" restrictor plate. If Driver Blue beats Driver Red at the Florida 500 by so much as a single inch of their front bumper, Driver Blue gets all 30 Championship Laps for that track. Driver Red gets absolutely nothing but a blown gasket, even if millions of fans in the Florida infield were waving Red flags. You don't get partial laps for finishing second, unless you are racing at the Nebraska or Maine speedways, which use a weird stage-racing format where they actually chop up the checkered flag and hand out the pieces based on who won turns 1, 2, and 3.

To hoist the big trophy, a driver needs to accumulate exactly 270 Championship Laps. Because of this point system, drivers don't spend much time tuning their engines at tracks where they know they’re going to get lapped, or at tracks where they are already three laps ahead. Instead, they spend all their time burning rubber at the "Swing Speedways"—tricky, slick tracks like Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin, where the track temperature changes constantly and anyone could end up in the winner's circle.

But wait, the race doesn't officially end when the cars cross the finish line in November. In December, the actual "Electors"—who are essentially highly partisan pit crew members—meet in the garage. These pit crew members are specifically chosen to carry the Championship Laps to the official scoring tower. Most of the time, the pit crew changes the tires exactly as the fans at their track demanded. But occasionally, you get a "Faithless Elector." This is a rogue tire-changer who decides, right in the middle of a four-tire stop, to slap a Goodyear on a car that was supposed to get Firestones, effectively handing a Championship Lap to a driver who wasn't even in the lead pack.

If nobody gets 270 Championship Laps because they all spun out in the infield grass and brought out the caution flag, the decision goes to the Race Officials in the House Garage. But they don't vote by driver; they vote by pit box.
